Second Waitematā Harbour crossing: NZ First leader is against latest Government plan

New Zealand Herald August 17, 2026

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters is clarifying claims his party did not support the latest business case investigating a second Auckland harbour crossing, confirming it endorsed the final decision but pushed for changes in Cabinet.

Peters told Ryan Bridge TODAY funding a new study into a second crossing was a “gross, shocking waste of money”.

The Government and Auckland Council have agreed to split a $1 million feasibility study into a second harbour crossing over Meola Reef, marking a formal consideration of Mayor Wayne Brown’s long-preferred bridge route.

Asked whether he agreed to the case when it was presented to Cabinet, Peters responded: “No, we said, ‘Look, this is not the way to go about it’. But if you don’t win, you don’t win.”

Elaborating on his comments following the interview, Peters said NZ First supported “the establishment of a senior expert to lead the exercise for Cabinet” but did not specifically task that person with leading a business case into Meola Reef.

Peters said he proposed the following changes:

NZ First remained concerned that the crossing debate risks pitting the Meola Reef option against a crossing adjacent to the existing bridge, Peters said.

“We say build a bridge and get over it.”

Yesterday’s announcement was described as a Cabinet decision, meaning all members would have supported the business case proposal. Cabinet collective responsibility requires members not to publicly disagree with decisions made by Cabinet.

Coalition parties have the ability to invoke an agree to disagree clause, however, this has not been referenced by NZ First following yesterday’s announcement.

Peters said he rejected this idea “completely”, saying the project should instead be put out to tender, with those tendering doing the exploratory work, as was happening at Marsden Point.

“Let them do all the work, let them make all the payments and let them do all the cost” – though he was open to partly subsidising that work.

He pointed to money “wasted” on Auckland light rail, the Skypath over the Harbour Bridge, the over-budget Pūhoi-Warkworth motorway, and Transmission Gully which “went broke in 2018 and when it was finished you had five different lots of tar seal and the tar seal had to be fixed up before the first car went on it”.

He said that $100m had already been spent consulting on a second harbour crossing.

“In any other country there would be people going to prison for that.”

Peters denied, when asked, that he was calling for Prime Minister Christopher Luxon and Transport Minister Chris Bishop to be jailed, but said there was a “massive lack of accountability”.

Later, Bishop confirmed that Cabinet had collectively agreed to the study “a couple of weeks ago”.

“Mr Peters is entitled to his view, obviously, but Cabinet’s made this decision.

“It’s the right thing to do, and we’ll be going ahead with it. And whoever’s in the hot seat in a year or so’s time – whether it’s me or whether it’s another transport minister – will have to advance this process.”

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown welcomed the study while criticising the millions already spent, saying we should “have a look at something sensible without getting too worried about worrywarts”.

Brown reiterated his belief that Auckland Council should lead decision-making on the crossing and was open to Peters’ suggestion of putting the project out for tender if it helped reduce costs and fast-track construction.

“I think it’s kind of better than what we’re doing, [which] is just tipping money into local consultants and getting nothing back.”

Richard Templer, chief executive of Engineering New Zealand, told Ryan Bridge TODAY it’s crucial that officials ensure whatever decision they advance is “very well-informed” and backed by Parliament and Aucklanders, arguing the country can’t afford to get it wrong.

“We don’t want decisions flip-flopping, because we know that has cost the country billions of dollars.”

The business case, announced by Luxon and Bishop yesterday, will investigate whether the natural lava flow at Point Chevalier offers a viable, lower-cost alternative to the multibillion-dollar tunnel options previously favoured by central government.

An independent expert will lead the project, reporting directly to ministers to resolve long-standing disputes over the crossing’s final design and funding.

Templer said the Meola Reef option’s viability would depend on the stability of the basalt rock and what lies underneath the lava flow.

“If you’re looking at a bridge, you need to know that the foundations the bridge will sit on are going to be able to take the weight of the bridge and the weight of the traffic.

“If you’re looking at a tunnel, you need to know what is under the water, whether it is going to be easy to tunnel through, whether it is going to be hard to tunnel through, and whether or not it’ll be able to take the load of all the water and seabed when you create a void underneath that.”

Remuera octogenarian jailed after ‘unprecedented volume’ of child abuse material uncovered

New Zealand Herald August 17, 2026

The man pleaded guilty to 15 charges.

A Remuera octogenarian has been handed a three-year jail term after admitting 15 charges related to possessing nearly 200,000 child abuse files across 15 devices.

However, the sentence was immediately appealed, and he has been released on bail pending a new hearing.

The graphic material was of an “unprecedented volume”, according to the prosecutor, and police were unable to catalogue the man’s abuse “collection” due to its size.

While the retired professional in his 80s failed in his bid to avoid a jail sentence, his lawyer Nathan Gibson successfully argued he should be granted permanent name suppression.

The reason for the name suppression order is also suppressed.

Auckland District Court Judge Andrea Manuel said at the man’s sentencing last Friday that no one “wants to sentence an elderly gentleman to a term of imprisonment”, but she told the court she must abide by the law.

She described the summary of facts as “disturbing”, and chose not to go into details, but said one child sexual abuse video showed a toddler in “pain or distress”.

Judge Manuel said the defendant used a “peer-to-peer” sharing platform, so his conduct wasn’t “passive” and he directly contributed to the wider circulation of material.

The prosecution had argued for a seven-year sentence starting point, while the defence sought a four-year start.

“It’s quite the gap,” Judge Manuel said.

Possessing objectionable material carries a maximum penalty of 10 years’ imprisonment.

While the defendant had no previous criminal convictions, Judge Manuel said he had received a discharge without conviction in 2006 for two male assaults female charges.

She gave the defendant a six-year starting point before considering discounts.

The only discount the defence and prosecution agreed on was a 25% reduction for his guilty plea.

Gibson had sought an 88% discount on the sentence, which would have resulted in a term of home detention.

However, prosecutor Rose Allison said just the 25% discount was appropriate.

“How can the defence submit 88% discount should apply when generally they do not exceed 40%? Well, let me explain,” Judge Manuel said.

She said his offending occurred before sentencing legislation was amended last year to cap total personal mitigating sentence discounts at 40%, so a higher potential discount was available.

Judge Manuel granted the man a 25% discount for his plea, 5% for his remorse and rehabilitation, 5% for his contribution to his profession and a 15% discount for his age and infirmity.

This resulted in three years’ jail.

Gibson immediately sought bail pending appeal, which Allison opposed but was granted.

Allison had earlier argued that a home-based sentence would be “manifestly inadequate” given the volume and nature of the files.

She said the defendant accepted that between December 2022 and April 2023 he downloaded more than 190,000 pieces of objectionable material.

She submitted it was an “exceptionally large” collection.

Allison told the court it was a serious case due to its volume, and nature.

“This isn’t an ordinary possession.”

Gibson, however, said this was an “exceptional case that warrants an exceptional outcome”.

He said 80% of the nearly 200,000 files fell into category B, which meant most of the content was not in the most serious category, A.

However, Judge Manuel was not moved by this argument.

“When I look at the sheer numbers [of category A content] compared to other cases, they’re still overwhelming.”

Gibson also submitted that there was no evidence his client had organised the content within the 15 hard drives.

He said his client was a man in his 80s, on the computer at home during a Covid lockdown, “pressing download and ending up with the volume of material that he has”.

“Prison would fall harder on a man like [the defendant].”

Katie Harris is an Auckland-based journalist who covers issues such as sexual assault, workplace misconduct, media, crime and justice. She joined the Herald in 2020.

This is, hands down, the most confronting thing I’ve seen on screen all year

Sydney Morning Herald August 18, 2026

Alex Gibney is no stranger to challenging material. But his film about the stabbing of Salman Rushdie takes some topping.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

As Salman Rushdie lay in hospital after being repeatedly stabbed on stage in August 2022, his wife Rachel Eliza Griffiths started filming. Asking if he was OK with that, he told her yes. “We need to document this.”

Now, Alex Gibney has turned that raw, unflinching and often hard-to-watch footage into Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie, one of the most confronting, but ultimately hopeful, movies you’ll ever see.

“On this film, I acted mostly as an editor,” says the prolific documentarian who won an Oscar (with Australian producer Eva Orner) for Taxi to the Dark Side in 2007 and has five Emmy wins to his name.

“My agent told me Salman and Eliza were interested in talking to me, and I learned they had this footage that Eliza took, starting on day five of his recovery and going right up to when they returned to the scene of the crime. And the first question I asked them was, ‘Why don’t you do it? No one knows more about what happened than you do’. And they said, ‘Well, that’s the problem. We feel too close to it. We want somebody else to come in and see if they can figure out a way to reckon with it.’”

Gibney pitched an approach informed by The Singing Detective, the 1986 BBC drama series written by Dennis Potter, in which Michael Gambon played a bed-bound writer in hospital whose medication produces a blurring of his imaginative world and his memories.

Despite its complex (and much-praised) structure, the show could be boiled down, says Gibney, to a pretty simple idea: a guy who is sick gets better, but along the way he reimagines his life through hallucinations and his detective fiction.

Rushdie, who had not yet decided to write his own account of the incident (his book Knife: Meditation on an Attempted Murder was released in August 2024), liked the idea, and the film Gibney has made – with Griffiths credited as executive producer and principal cinematographer – serves both as an account of the attack and its aftermath and as a meditation on Rushdie’s life more broadly.

Knife opens with a recreation of the attack, with Rushdie asking in voiceover, “Why didn’t I fight back?” It’s a shocking way to start, but it’s nothing compared to what follows.

The Booker Prize winner was in a chair on the stage of the Chautauqua Institution in New York State, about to be interviewed, when a man armed with a knife rushed up the steps and lunged at him. The attacker, Hadi Matar, stabbed the novelist 15 times, landing blows in his neck, stomach, chest and thigh. One of them struck Rushdie, who was 76 at the time, in his right eye (he has lost all sight in it).

Matar had been inspired by the fatwa issued by Iran in 1989 in response to Rushdie’s novel The Satanic Verses, which Ayatollah Khomeini and his fellow clerics had deemed blasphemous. (Iran’s position on the fatwa has since become somewhat ambiguous, but it has never officially been rescinded. Last month a trial on terrorism charges against Matar – who has already been convicted of attempted murder – began in Buffalo, New York.)

The film also includes real footage of the attack, which was only released during Matar’s first trial in February 2025. It’s horrendous in its brutality, and Gibney admits he wasn’t sure that he should even include it.

“I mean, for a documentarian, it would be very hard not to show the actual crime, but I did ponder that maybe we shouldn’t,” he says. What got him over the line was the footage Griffiths had shot of her and Rushdie returning to Chautauqua, “and within that context it seemed to make sense to show it”.

The most challenging scenes in the film, though, are probably the shots of Rushdie’s horribly disfigured eyeball, bulging from its socket, occluded, pointing wildly out of focus. “Trust me,” says Gibney, “in a theatre you can hear the whole audience go ‘aagh’. It’s very difficult to watch.”

There was never any chance of not including that footage, though. “Both of them [Rushdie and Griffiths] felt very strongly that they wanted to show this is what terrorism looks like.”

For all that Griffiths’ footage was the rock on which the film is built, Gibney knew he had to go beyond it to tell the story he had in mind.

“Too much of that, and it’s only about his physical recovery, rather than a deeper kind of mental recovery,” he says. “And once you enter the mind, it’s a chaotic and unpredictable place, and you have to sort of go with the flow.”

In archival footage, interviews from across the decades and in his own scripted narration, Rushdie reflects on being an outsider in his own family in Mumbai, of feeling the lash of racism at the English boarding school (Rugby) to which he was sent by his father when he was 14, of the cold shoulder some in the literary establishment turned on him when Iran called for his murder, with the offer of a massive bounty (starting at $1 million, it eventually rose to $6 million).

There’s a sense overall of a man wounded many times in his life, and of his attempt to stitch himself back together in spite of it all. Whatever you might think of Rushdie, it’s impossible not to be moved by his resilience, his unflinching commitment to free speech, and his refusal of hatred.

Ultimately, Gibney says, the film he made “wasn’t about the record of an attack, it was about how you reckon with the attack. And one way of reckoning with it is to go back to that moment and relive it in a way that you can be kind of outside it and not succumb to overwhelming dread.

“There’s a kind of curative aspect to it,” Gibney adds. “This is what recovery looks like.”

Knife: The Attempted Murder of Salman Rushdie screens at the Melbourne International Film Festival on August 18 and 20 and at Sydney Festival of Dangerous Ideas on August 20. Details: miff. com. au and festivalofdangerousideas. com

Rubin Colwill’s last-gasp free-kick earns Cardiff dramatic point against Wrexham

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 21:32:53 GMT

Rubin Colwill scored a ferocious equaliser with almost the final kick of the match to earn Cardiff a 1-1 Championship draw with Wrexham.

Wrexham appeared to have the Welsh derby bragging rights sewn up as the contest ticked into the eighth minute of added time at Cardiff City Stadium.

But George Dobson brought down Joel Colwill on the edge of the box, and his brother Rubin stepped up to lash a brilliant free-kick over the wall and past Anthony Patterson in the Wrexham goal.

Colwill’s strike cancelled out Kieffer Moore’s third-minute effort, the former Cardiff forward continuing his habit of scoring against his former employers – his seventh goal against the Bluebirds.

Wrexham had 18 goal attempts to 11 and, in truth, should have prevented any late anxiety by putting the game beyond the hosts back at this level after a season in League One.

Cardiff’s defensive resources had been stretched by injuries to Calum Chambers, Dylan Lawlor and Will Fish, so much so that the usual left-back Joel Bagan was switched inside to partner Gabriel Osho in the heart of defence.

The new-look partnership was exposed immediately after Cardiff only managed to clear a Lewis O’Brien free-kick as far as Danny Imray, and his ball forward caught the hosts napping.

Osho played Moore onside and the striker broke beyond Bagan to rifle the ball above Nathan Trott’s head for his first goal since February, ending his run of 11 Wrexham games without scoring.

Trott tipped over Callum Doyle’s header as Cardiff appeared to struggle to get to grips with the pace of Championship football. But the Bluebirds slowly improved and had a good spell midway through the first half after Zak Vyner left a back pass short and Patterson reacted smartly to beat Yousef Salech to the loose ball.

Jack Moylan then scooped over and Patterson made a comfortable save from Cian Ashford after some slick Cardiff passing.

Wrexham went close to a second when Moore rose well from an O’Brien cross and skimmed the crossbar with a header. Imray’s scuffed shot then forced a save from Trott, although the ball appeared to be heading wide anyway.

Just as they had at the start of the game, Cardiff switched off after the restart. Ollie Rathbone’s ball inside found Doyle, but Trott was alive at the near post to save with his foot. Trott made a more comfortable stop from Nathan Broadhead before Doyle lashed a rasping drive past him and on to a post.

Cardiff sent on the Colwill brothers just after the hour mark to try to shift momentum in their favour, and Moylan saw his deflected effort drift just wide.

Dominic Hyam headed against his own crossbar, but Cardiff kept pushing and ultimately denied Wrexham their first win in the Welsh capital since 1992.

Burnham scraps restrictions on disabled people’s bus passes in England

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 21:30:05 GMT

Move means holders will be able to travel free on local services at any time of day or night from April next year

Disabled people across England will be able to use their free bus passes at any time of day from next April, as Andy Burnham expands a policy he introduced as mayor of Greater Manchester.

The prime minister has said the current weekday restrictions on when disabled people can use their bus passes will be removed from 1 April 2027. Their passes are valid only between 9.30am and 11pm on weekdays, although some councils pay to allow people free travel outside those hours.

The change means disabled bus pass holders will be able to travel free on local bus services where the pass applies at any time of day or night. The charity Mencap welcomed the measures, noting that disabled people often struggle with the cost of living as well as the cost of their disability.

Burnham is putting up £60m in funding for the change, with £40m coming from the Department for Work and Pensions and £20m from the Department for Transport.

Government sources said the funding has no set end date and was not a one-off payment. They said the change would take seven months to introduce because it must be passed by parliament, and the April start date gave local transport authorities time to prepare.

Burnham is on the second week of his summer tour during which he is focusing on the cost of living. The disabled bus pass policy has been in place in Greater Manchester since March.

“Buses are a lifeline for so many people – making it easier to get to work, education and healthcare,” Burnham said. “It’s simply not right that many disabled people cannot travel using their pass during certain times of the day. So we’re fixing that. Disabled people will now have unlimited free bus travel 24/7.

“I did it before in Greater Manchester and I’m proud to do it now for the whole country. This is part of our ongoing action to bring back hope and give people some much needed breathing space on the cost of living.”

Ministers say the move will help disabled people get into work, education and training as well as helping with the cost of living.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said the change would end a postcode lottery under which disabled people got different levels of support depending on where they lived.

The government says the measure is part of wider plans to make bus travel cheaper, including keeping the £2 fare cap throughout 2027 and giving under-16s free bus travel this summer.

A New York state ⁠judge on Monday ⁠effectively ​postponed Luigi Mangione’s trial on murder and weapons charges over ⁠the 2024 killing of a health insurance company CEO, after Mangione pleaded ⁠guilty last week to separate federal charges.

The ​trial had ‌previously been ‌scheduled to begin on September 8. Mangione ‌has pleaded not guilty to the state charges. Mangione’s lawyers on Friday asked New York state justice Gregory Carro, who is overseeing the state case, ‌to dismiss the charges.

They argued that Mangione should not have to ​be punished for the same conduct twice, under New York’s law prohibiting double jeopardy.

In a brief written order on ⁠Monday, Carro gave prosecutors until 9 October ​to ​respond to Mangione’s ​motion. The judge set Mangione’s next ​appearance in ‌state court ​for ​10 December, meaning the trial will not go forward next month.

Mangione, 28, confessed that he shot and killed Brian Thompson outside a New York City hotel on 4 December 2024.

He had a dispute with UnitedHealthcare, the US insurance giant Thompson ran, about his treatment for severe back pain and, he told the court last week, had problems with “navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system and witnessing similar experiences of countless others”.

In his federal case, Mangione faced stalking charges, after other charges, including murder, were dropped.

A spokesperson for Manhattan district attorney, Alvin Bragg, who brought the state charges against Mangione, referred to a Friday statement indicating that the office was prepared ‌to litigate the defense motions. Mangione’s defense lawyers declined to comment.

Mangione entered his guilty plea in the federal case without reaching an agreement with prosecutors, and there was ​no guarantee that his acceptance of responsibility would result in leniency at sentencing.

Sentencing is due in the federal case on 18 December. Federal prosecutors said on Friday that they intend to seek a life sentence, the maximum allowable.

In the state case, Mangione would face 25 years to life in prison if convicted of second-degree murder.

If Carro decides to dismiss the state ⁠case, it would eliminate the possibility of Mangione having to serve consecutive prison sentences in the ​two cases.

Bennett Gershman, a law professor ​at Pace University in New York, said it ​was unlikely Carro would dismiss the case on double jeopardy grounds.

New York state’s double jeopardy law ​carves out exceptions for crimes ‌that have different elements ​or are aimed at preventing “very ​different kinds of harm or evil”.

The federal stalking charges to which Mangione pleaded guilty to still require intent to kill but do not require that the death occurs.

“The elements in stalking and the elements of murder are very, very distinguishable,” Gershman said.

Buried With Michael Sheen review – this vital look at a toxic waste scandal is deeply enraging TV

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 21:00:04 GMT

The actor does a brilliant job of probing the alleged dumping of ‘forever chemicals’ in Wales. After grilling a stranger for two days, his investigation turns up horrible incidents – including potential links to cancer cases

You may scoff at celebrity-fronted documentaries, but there’s no need to moan about Buried With Michael Sheen, an investigation into how toxic “forever chemicals” were dumped in Welsh quarries in the middle of the 20th century. Much of our knowledge of the subject comes from a filmed interview given nearly 10 years ago by the environmental campaigner Douglas Gowan, who, after decades of trying to raise awareness, had only weeks to live and wanted to divulge all he had learned. The person behind the camera and asking the questions? Sheen.

The actor and director is a little coy about how or why he came to spend two days – two days! – grilling a stranger to create the most valuable document we have about an underappreciated injustice. He says something about stumbling across Gowan online during a career lull and wanting to know more. But however it happened, the fact is that the best qualified person to present this two-parter is the award-winning Hollywood star, so here he is.

And very good he is, too: passionate about the outrage, but sober in his pursuit of truth. It proves to be a story that keeps throwing up moments and characters for which a scriptwriter would congratulate themselves. Sheen fits right in.

We’re talking about the now defunct American agrochemicals giant Monsanto, which after the second world war cornered the market in, shall we say, controversial chemical innovations. Agent Orange, DDT and Roundup were all made by Monsanto, as were polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) – indestructible compounds that were hailed as miracle chemicals until they were discovered to be toxic and carcinogenic. From the 1940s to the late 1970s, PCBs were made at the Monsanto plant in Newport, the city where Sheen spent some of his childhood.

The question is what was done with the factory’s waste. Gowan deduced that it was buried in landfills across south Wales – in a way that he thought allowed PCBs to leech into the surrounding water and soil.

Sheen travels first to the village of Ynysddu, where the two councillors who have spoken out most on this issue are both called Jan and are thus known as “the two Jans”. One of the Jans relays testimony from villagers who remember lorries arriving at night at the nearby quarry – now an eerie patch of unloved grass, ringed by trees – and leaving behind a jelly-like substance on the roads that children would play with the next morning. At a meeting inside Ynysddu Progressive Workingmans Club, residents describe the phenomenon that has convinced them that, decades later, something is still wrong: dogs that are walked in the woods keep dying of cancer.

As is customary with these scandals, the narrative repeatedly turns up horrible localised problems that those affected are sure they know the cause of, even if proof of direct causation is hard to find. Next, Sheen jets to Anniston, Alabama, formerly the site of Monsanto’s main PCB factory in the US. A paediatrician working there today says she has seen an unusual amount of birth defects, including children born without eyes or with their intestines on the outside of their bodies.

Sheen meets the attorney Donald Stewart, who in 1993 sued Monsanto on behalf of the town, securing a $300m settlement. Stewart shares internal Monsanto memos from as long ago as 1949 that suggest the firm knew how dangerous PCBs were. How did Monsanto think it could get away with endangering the Anniston public, Sheen asks? This inquiry produces a breathtaking moment. “If you look at this area, they’re working people,” Stewart replies. Suddenly, this courtroom bruiser is choking back tears. “They wouldn’t be able to fight back.”

Back at home, Sheen pores over parliament’s Hansard transcripts with Dan Ashby and Lucy Taylor, the married investigative duo who present the BBC Radio 4 podcast series Buried. They reveal that, in 1973, shortly after the production of PCBs in Anniston was stopped, a government minister in Westminster was traducing Gowan from the dispatch box, insinuating that he had doctored his evidence. The parliamentary debate followed a Sunday Times expose by the journalist Peter Pringle, who used Gowan as a source.

From there, Sheen dons wellies and embarks on a project to test the soil near the landfills, accompanied by an environmental scientist and – because although this tale is enragingly serious, it keeps turning up delightful quirks – a vicar. The Gowan of today is the Rev Paul Cawthorne, whose interest was sparked by a deathbed confession from a parishioner who used to drive trucks filled with barrels of seething crud.

The PCBs affair has been rumbling on for years without many firm answers being obtained, but that may change in next week’s concluding episode: you wouldn’t bet against the actor, the vicar, the podcasting spouses and the two Jans cracking the case.

Buried With Michael Sheen aired on BBC Two and is available on BBC iPlayer

Tupac Shakur murder trial: prosecutors allege Duane Davis plotted killing to avenge nephew

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 20:57:30 GMT

Shakur’s entourage was filmed beating Orlando ‘Baby Lane’ Anderson, Davis’s nephew, in September 1996

What we know about Tupac Shakur’s death

The trial of a former gang leader accused of orchestrating the 1996 killing of rap star Tupac Shakur began in a Las Vegas courtroom on Monday, featuring testimony from a witness to the shooting and a former police officer.

Duane “Keffe D” Davis is on trial for murder for his alleged role in the shooting of Shakur, who died after a drive-by shooting. Prosecutors allege Davis was the “on-the-ground, on-site commander of the effort to kill Tupac” and that he planned the shooting in retaliation for Shakur’s entourage attacking Davis’s nephew.

Davis has pleaded not guilty, though he acknowledged a role in the shooting in a 2019 memoir that authorities have said is key to the case against the 63-year-old. He is the only living witness from the car that fired shots at Shakur.

Last week, a jury of six men and 10 women was selected in the trial, which is expected to last about a month.

Davis entered the courtroom in a blue suit and tie and scanned the audience to see who was there before sitting next to his lawyer, Michael Sanft, once the jury was sworn in and seated on Monday morning.

Members of Shakur’s family, including his stepbrother Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur, sat quietly in the front row of the courtroom behind prosecutors.

Binu Palal, the chief deputy district attorney, showed jurors a picture of the Mike Tyson fight with the date “September 7, 1996” and showed video of Shakur’s entourage beating Orlando “Baby Lane” Anderson, Davis’s nephew.

“Let’s be clear, Duane Davis did not pull the trigger. But he did plan the shooting in retaliation of the beating of his nephew,” Palal said. “Remarkably, you will learn that from Duane Davis himself.”

Palal showed multiple video clips and played audio of Davis describing his alleged role in the incident and anger toward Shakur for the attack on his nephew.

Sanft, the defense lawyer, meanwhile, said that after 30 years, investigators still have very little evidence to prove their case.

“At the end ​of the day you have to ask yourself, is what they are saying truth ‌or fiction?” Sanft told the jury.

Sanft argued that while Davis spoke about the killing to different law enforcement agencies over the years, including the FBI, they did not follow up because they did not believe what he said was credible, the defense attorney said.

The trial is a major development in the case that for decades was unsolved.

On 7 September 1996, the rap icon was attacked just off the Las Vegas strip as he headed to an afterparty with the Death Row Records founder, Marion “Suge” Knight. While traveling in the vehicle, a Cadillac pulled up next to Shakur’s vehicle and fired eight shots. Shakur was hospitalized for his injuries and died days later.

Shakur’s killing spawned countless conspiracy theories as well as books and documentaries seeking to determine who was responsible for his death. But a fuller picture of what may have occurred that night has emerged in recent years as Davis, who was the last surviving passenger in the Cadillac, began speaking publicly.

Earlier in the evening Shakur had attended the Tyson fight at the MGM Grand Hotel and afterward was involved in a physical confrontation with Davis’s nephew and several others.

Davis sought retribution for Anderson and allegedly obtained a gun with the intent to “hunt down” Shakur and confront Knight. The incident unfolded quickly, Davis wrote.

“No words were exchanged, the time for talking had passed, the shit was on! Tupac made an erratic move and began to reach down beneath his seat. It was the first and only time in my life that I could relate to the police command to, ‘Keep your hands where I can see them.’ Instead, Pac pulled out a strap, and that’s when the fireworks started. One of my guys from the back seat grabbed the Glock and started bustin’ back,” he wrote.

Prosecutors have said that Davis’s tell-all book and public statements ultimately revived the Las Vegas investigation.

“Had he decided to never write the book, he would not, probably, have ever been prosecuted for the crime,” prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo recently said.

His attorneys sought to exclude the book from trial by arguing that he and his co-author exaggerated in an effort to “falsely place himself at the center of it all for personal gain”. A judge denied the request.

The first witness called by prosecutors was Garry Dale, a former Las Vegas officer who pulled over Shakur and Knight on the night of the shooting. He said he stopped the car because it lacked a license plate on the back, and that the interaction was “congenial”. The officer recounted later riding in the ambulance with Shakur after the shooting, saying he tried to convince the rapper to name his assailants, but that Shakur responded: “No, we’ll take care of it.”

Prosecutors’ second witness was Ingrid Stokes, a woman who was in a car with friends near Shakur’s car at the time of the shooting. Stokes’s car and Shakur’s car were both going to the same club, she said. “We heard the gunshots … all hell broke loose,” she said. Stokes added that she didn’t see who was in the car that fired on Skakur, and that she later spoke to police who were “rude” and “treated us like suspects”.

Stokes said she didn’t think she had any valuable information to share with officers, and that she and her friends had fear at the time about talking to officers and being labeled as “snitches”.

Tens of thousands of people gathered in Trafalgar Square in London to remember and pay tribute to Jason Arday, the former Cambridge professor who died on Friday.

Stand Up to Racism, which organised the vigil, estimated that 30,000 mourners had gathered in the square to listen to emotional speeches from MPs, friends and campaigners on Arday’s life and legacy and join in a minute’s silence. Many were dressed in black and held flowers, which they were asked to leave beneath Nelson’s column. People also carried placards reading “rest in power”.

Arday, 41, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to his home in south London on Friday. He had just resigned from his role as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge, after widespread scrutiny over accusations of plagiarism, which he rejected, and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.

Opening the event, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, the local MP for Arday’s family in Clapham and Brixton Hill, said: “I’m going to look around you and look at how many people have come tonight.

“That tells you what Jason meant. He held doors open behind him. He kept them open and thousands of us walked through. That is why this place is full tonight. And I know that all of you are grieving. I know there are many people that aren’t even here.”

Ribeiro-Addy asked that people respect the privacy of Arday’s family, who “lost their son, their brother. Not a professor, not a headline, not a symbol.” She asked that they be given “time, space and quiet” to grieve.

She concluded the vigil by reading out a statement from Arday’s family. They said: “The public cruelty Jason was subjected to was too much for any man to bear. The outpouring of love, support, and grief since his death means so much to us. Although it is bittersweet now, kindness is needed in life, not just in death.”

Many speeches focused on the role of the media in Arday’s death. Diane Abbott, MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, said there had been 249 articles about him within three weeks. “He must have felt that if he resigned, the attacks on him would stop. But in fact, they got even worse,” she said. “This is a vicious campaign.”

The British singer Beverley Knight performed her song Keep This Fire Burning and Jermain Jackman, who won The Voice in 2014, performed a cover of Coldplay’s Fix You, requested by Arday’s family. The MPs Zack Polanski and Jeremy Corbyn were also in attendance.

Simon Woolley, who was a mentor to Arday at Cambridge, said that when he had seen Arday shortly before his death, “we knew Jason was suffering” and feeling “hounded”, and he had hugged him. “We told him he was loved,” Woolley said.

Remembering Arday as a “wonderful man [who] never stole a bag of crisps”, he urged that there “be some reckoning” after Arday’s death.

Windrush campaigner Patrick Vernon said the evening was the time to “pay our respects and to stand in solidarity with his grieving family”. “Let’s remember his life, his scholarship, his achievements, his determination and his humanity and the people that he inspired,” he said.

But he added that it would be important to reflect on the role of “racism, institutional responsibility, accountability and the treatment of black families and black men” in Arday’s death, as well as why the “duty of care” to an autistic man known to be vulnerable had failed, potentially through a public inquiry.

Samira Ali, an organiser at Stand Up to Racism, read out a statement from a close friend and colleague of Arday, which said: “Prof Jason, the words kind, beautiful and gentle seem to orbit so many dedications to him and they are not wrong. But in truth, words will never quite capture the type of person Prof Jason was or what he meant to people.”

The statement referenced Arday’s work setting up mentoring schemes and mental health support for students and academics of colour. It said: “He worked tirelessly to inspire all students from marginalised backgrounds to believe that academia could also belong to them. He did not inspire one or two people to do a PhD; there are dozens of us over generations who have dreamed and are now doctors and soon-to-be professors because of him.”

The Fifa chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, has been sacked after openly criticising Gianni Infantino’s ill-fated plan to sell parts of the World Cup to private investors.

In a significant development at the pinnacle of world football’s deeply troubled governing body, Lamour has departed less than two years after joining from a previous role at Uefa. Lamour had also made clear that he would countenance losing his job as a consequence of opposing the plan, which was shelved hours after he spoke out on 31 July. “If that means I lose my job, then so be it,” he said in a statement. “I will understand and respect that decision. The precise circumstances of his sacking are unclear but the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, informed staff in an email that Lamour would be leaving the organisation.

A Fifa spokesperson said: “Fifa can confirm that the working relationship between Fifa and Kevin Lamour as Fifa’s chief operating officer has ended on 17 August 2026. Fifa thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter.”

In the statement that appears to have expedited his departure, Lamour also said his colleagues “deserve better than contempt and intimidation”. He added: “My feeling is that we all want to be proud to work for Fifa, and today, unfortunately, it seems that is no longer the case for many of us.” On the same day one of Infantino’s senior advisers, Carlos Cordeiro, resigned in protest at Infantino’s proposals.

Lamour had been Uefa’s deputy secretary general before joining Fifa, and had first joined the European body in 2007. Trump’s move to gut South Korea alliance is ‘inane, haphazard decision’, lawmakers say

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 19:11:26 GMT

US president’s abrupt order to scale back joint exercises with Seoul is meant to ‘flatter’ North Korea’s dictator, top Democrat says

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump’s move to gut Washington’s 73-year-old military alliance with Seoul has been called “inane” and “shortsighted” as lawmakers warned it risked strengthening Russia’s hand in Ukraine.

The US president abruptly ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint exercises with South Korea just days after North Korea test-fired ballistic missiles, justifying the decision by citing his “very good relationship” with Kim Jong-Un, the nuclear-armed dictator such exercises exist to deter.

Trump announced the order on social media, directing the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, to scale back Ulchi Freedom Shield, an 11-day exercise due to run from 17 to 27 August involving about 18,000 South Korean troops rehearsing scenarios including missile strikes, drone incursions and cyber-attacks.

Trump framed the decision as a courtesy to Kim, writing that the drills “send a signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to a country he described as “unthreatening and respectful”, despite North Korea’s continued missile testing and its expanding nuclear arsenal.

Democrats in Congress said the move handed Kim a propaganda win for nothing, while an ally was left paying the price for a war in the Middle East it never agreed to fight.

Jack Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate armed services committee, called it “another inane, haphazard decision by President Trump and his chaotic administration”.

“When President Trump cuts military exercises to flatter a dictator or punishes South Korea for declining to join a war he started, all of our allies – and adversaries – think that America’s commitments are negotiable,” Reed said in a statement, describing the move as punishing Korea “for no reason beyond Trump’s ego”.

Reed’s warning was echoed by Mark Kelly of Arizona, who sits on the same committee, and argued that the drills were not symbolic but the basis of the alliance’s ability to function in a crisis. “North and South Korea are still technically at war,” Kelly said. “Our ability to help defend our ally against the North Koreans is because our forces are well trained and able to coordinate with the South Koreans. Hollowing out these joint exercises is shortsighted and a mistake.”

In the Oval Office on Monday, Trump claimed Kim had responded to his overtures, but did not provide details. “I understand him,” the president said. “He understands me.”

The alliance Trump is now unwinding dates to the 1953 Mutual Defense Treaty signed after the Korean war armistice. Roughly 28,500 American troops remain stationed in South Korea, backed by a combined US-South Korean command structure and Washington’s pledge to extend its nuclear umbrella over Seoul.

Despite Trump calling North Korea “unthreatening”, his own administration’s 2026 Annual Threat Assessment describes an “increasingly confident North Korean regime”, warning that its weapons of mass destruction, conventional forces and cyber operations threaten the US, South Korea and Japan. His former director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, testified in March that “North Korea’s ICBMs [intercontinental ballistic missiles] can already reach US soil”.

Trump also tied his decision to the Iran war, saying he was unhappy that Seoul had declined to join the US military campaign against Iran, a campaign that has drained US missile stockpiles and, after Tehran shut the strait of Hormuz, helped push up prices at home. He acknowledged the two issues had little to do with one another, even as he punished Seoul over both.

“While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks’!” Trump wrote.

Andy Kim, the New Jersey senator who sits on the Senate foreign relations committee, said linking the exercises to that refusal exposed a troubling attitude toward a key partner.

“Our alliance with the Republic of Korea is critical for US security and prosperity – and I am concerned that President Trump’s post today suggests a disregard for this relationship,” Kim said. “South Korea is an essential partner in peace and security in a part of the world filled with risk; we should treat them that way instead of venting frustration on social media.”

It is not the first time Trump has treated the drills as a bargaining chip. After his 2018 summit with Kim in Singapore, he suspended major exercises outright, calling them costly and provocative, before they were quietly restored once nuclear diplomacy with Pyongyang broke down.

The dispute comes as Seoul has spent much of the past year charting its own path on the Middle East. In February, South Korea’s government said it had “grave concern” over Israeli measures expanding control in the occupied West Bank and urged Israel to “reverse its decisions immediately”.

In April, Seoul’s ambassador to the United Nations told the security council that any unilateral annexation of Palestinian territory “should be revoked”. Lee Jae-myung, the president of South Korea, has twice clashed publicly with Israel: in April over remarks he made comparing footage of an Israeli soldier’s treatment of a Palestinian man’s body to the Holocaust, and in May after two South Korean activists were detained on a Gaza-bound aid mission.

Thom Tillis, the outgoing Republican senator from North Carolina, chimed in making the point that the butterfly effect of Trump’s decision would inadvertently benefit Russia.

“South Korea has been a solid military ally for over 70 years that possesses exquisite military capabilities,” Tillis wrote on social media. “Reducing joint exercises with South Korea does nothing more than free up thousands of North Korea’s troops to support Putin’s systematic kidnapping, torture, rape and murder of innocent Ukrainian citizens.”

The Chelsea chair, Todd Boehly, and director Mark Walter are considering selling their shares in the club to the majority owners, Clearlake Capital, in a deal that would give the private equity company complete control at Stamford Bridge.

Clearlake, whose investment is managed by Behdad Eghbali and José E Feliciano, already owns more than 60% of Chelsea, but in an unusual arrangement agreed when buying the club from Roman Abramovich four years ago, they share operational control with a consortium led by Boehly, who along with Walter and Hansjörg Wyss each own about 13%.

The two ownership groups have been locked in a stalemate for almost two years when reports first emerged that they were seeking to buy each other out following a disagreement over strategy, particularly regarding their plans for a new stadium.

Discussions over a potential deal, which would value the club at more than £5bn, have resumed over the past few weeks however, as first reported by the Financial Times, as Walter is seeking to raise funds to pay off insurers following a US federal investigation over alleged tax fraud.

Walter is being investigated by the US Department of Justice over $21bn in loans which it has been alleged were not disclosed to state insurance regulators, which has led to the sudden sale of assets to pay down some of the loans. Walter last week sold the Los Angeles Lakers to Josh ⁠Kushner and Bob Iger ⁠for $12.5bn just a year after buying the NBA franchise for $10bn, leading to speculation that the 66-year-old may also seek to exit Chelsea.

Boehly and Walter are close friends as well as longstanding business partners, having previously invested together in the LA Dodgers Major League Baseball team and the LA Sparks WNBA franchise.

Together with Wyss, the pair control 38% of Chelsea through Blueco 22 Holdings, although it is unclear whether the Swiss billionaire is also willing to sell. Under the terms of their £2.5bn purchase from Abramovich after the Russian was sanctioned by the UK government following the invasion of Ukraine however, none of Chelsea’s shareholders can sell to a third party without the consent of their partners.

An external sale is therefore unlikely, putting Clearlake in a strong position to gain the complete control it has been seeking for some time, although Boehly and Walter will demand a significant premium on the £325m they paid for their shares four years ago.

A sale by Boehly and Walter would leave Clearlake with more than 86% of Chelsea’s shares and effective control of the club, including the bid to build a new stadium, which they want to locate at Stamford Bridge.

Walter has been a silent and barely visible partner at Chelsea, but Boehly was the public face of the club following the 2022 takeover and acted as interim sporting director during that year’s summer transfer window, leading the purchase of players such as Raheem Sterling and Marc Cucurella.

Boehly stepped back from that hands-on role after 12 months, with Eghbali taking more operational control on behalf of Clearlake, but has often been blamed by Chelsea fans for the side’s underperformance.

Boehly was due to stand down as chair at the end of the season, with a Clearlake representative to replace him for the next five years under the terms of the ownership agreement.

The Guardian view on Jason Arday: a tragedy that demands reflection

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 18:24:19 GMT

Legitimate scrutiny became entangled with a racial argument about merit and diversity. His death raises questions about how society treats black success and failure

The tragic death of Jason Arday raises serious questions about race, institutional authority and what happens to people in a society increasingly organised around public reputation. Arday, who resigned earlier this month as a professor at the University of Cambridge, was found dead at his home last week. He was 41. His family and friends have lost somebody they loved and cared for. Arday had publicly said that the scrutiny of allegations concerning his academic work and claims he had made about his life was taking a profound toll. That he then died amid an intense and continuing media examination of his life is deeply troubling.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, was right to call this “a moment for reflection”. This does not mean suppressing difficult questions, ignoring why there remain a pitifully small number of black professors in British universities, or attacking legitimate journalism. But in a polarised world it should see the media ask how proper scrutiny can widen into something more encompassing; how race affects the meaning attached to an individual’s alleged failings; and whether separate valid stories can, via social media, have an overwhelming effect. In Arday’s case, alleged shortcomings in his record rapidly became weaponised by the right in an argument about diversity and black academic advancement.

Arday’s story – an autistic child from a council estate who became a Cambridge professor aged just 37 – was remarkable. The university publicised the symbolic dimensions of his appointment as a young, black, neurodivergent man. He had been accused of plagiarism in his doctoral thesis – allegations an earlier Liverpool John Moores University investigation had not upheld. His latest accuser, Nathan Cofnas, had advanced ideas widely condemned as racist, making it impossible to regard his intervention as neutral. However, there was a clear public interest case for investigating such allegations.

The Guardian sought to establish what was true. That is the proper function of journalism. Reporters were contacted by Arday over a year ago and worked extensively to verify what he had told them. In many instances they could not. It was right for the Guardian to publish its investigation, and it is wrong that the journalists who did their job responsibly are now being subjected to an onslaught of abuse. Cambridge, which has many of its own questions to answer, announced that it would hold an internal inquiry. In its journalism, the Guardian sought to meet tests of importance and proportionality, covering the issue with nuance. This could not be said of much of the rightwing media and its social media outriders.

Arday became an exhibit in an ideological, almost Trumpian campaign against diversity and inclusion. The allegations were no longer simply about one academic’s behaviour or his past record. They were used to suggest that Arday had never deserved to be there – and that he had only been advanced because of his race. The attacks were relentless, often partisan, and amplified without respite online.

This is racism at work. White academics are generally allowed to fail as individuals. Black ones are not. Arday may have had questions to answer; that did not make black academics collectively answerable for him. A society committed to equality must allow black people the same freedom as everyone else: to be flawed, to make mistakes, and even to fail, without their failure becoming an indictment of their race.

The Guardian view on a vibrant summer for British athletics: inspiring a generation

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 18:23:57 GMT

Amy Hunt’s record haul of four golds in Birmingham showcased the sport’s appeal. More can be done to ensure it gets its fair share of the limelight

To win one gold medal is impressive. To win two indicates a certain relentlessness. To win four in the space of one remarkable week of athletics may ensure further recognition for Amy Hunt as the BBC’s sports personality of the year. Ms Hunt’s record‑breaking achievement in winning the 100m, 200m, women’s relay and mixed relay at the first European championships to be held in Britain was an exhibition of world-class sprinting for the ages.

Her triumph capped a week which reminded us that there is more to sporting life than football. By winning an 11th medal, Dina Asher-Smith became the most successful athlete in the history of the competition. And on Friday, at a packed Alexander athletics stadium in Birmingham, the crowd savoured a contest and burgeoning rivalry that recalled the halcyon days of Sebastian Coe and Steve Ovett. Audrey Werro, the young Swiss star, and Keely Hodgkinson, Team GB’s Olympic champion, produced a thrillingly intense women’s 800m final, which Werro won with a time that broke a European record set in 1982.

Athletics fans should relish the moment. The walls are closing in as another Premier League season begins, sucking the oxygen of publicity away from rival sports. An expanded World Cup, and the fallout from plans to sell a stake in the competition to private equity, made it seem as if football never went away. But it has been a stellar couple of months for British athletes.

Josh Kerr’s shattering of the one-mile world record, in front of 60,000 spectators at July’s London Diamond League meet, was the sporting event of the summer until Hunt arguably trumped it. There was also a successful salvage operation in Scotland. Glasgow’s staging of the Commonwealth Games at short notice, after the original Australian hosts pulled out, rescued the event from limbo.

The only downside was that the rich talent on display did not, at times, get the fanfare it deserved. Glasgow’s efforts went somewhat under the national radar after cost-conscious organisers rejected a low offer from the BBC and sold rights to the Discovery channel. The boost that terrestrial coverage can give was shown by an audience estimated to be in the region of 4 million for the epic runoff between Werro and Hodgkinson.

Birmingham, however, has had its own problems as cameras panned across acres of empty seats in the early part of last week. The former athlete and BBC commentator Steve Cram has been among those to question high ticket prices, and there was a notable lack of cut-price deals to attract the next generation of athletics fans. The promotion and marketing of the event in Birmingham itself, in stark contrast with the 2022 Commonwealth Games, was somewhat underwhelming.

For a sport which can produce such scintillating moments of concentrated drama, and in which male and female athletes enjoy a genuine equality of esteem, that is a shame. British athletics is enjoying a golden era, and sassy personalities such as Hunt – a Cambridge graduate who once described herself as “an ­academic badass and a track ­goddess” – have a charismatic appeal.

The chosen motto of the London 2012 Olympics was “Inspire a generation”. As the likes of Hunt, Hodgkinson and Kerr do just that, more can be done to support and promote their efforts. Football may now be back. But Britain’s stars of track and field jumped through their annual summer window of opportunity to stunning effect.

Reform’s Tice accused of misinformation after urging people to enjoy heatwaves

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 18:06:13 GMT

Nurses, medical experts and green campaigners reject party deputy leader’s dismissal of efforts to reach net zero

Reform’s deputy leader has been accused of spreading misinformation after he dismissed efforts to tackle the climate crisis and urged British people to enjoy the warmth of the recent heatwaves.

Richard Tice prompted a backlash from nurses, medical experts and green campaigners on Monday after he told a press conference he believed it was “arrogant” to try to stop the climate emergency, while encouraging people to focus on upsides such as better English wine.

Asked about the recent extreme heat, Tice told a press conference: “Of course, the climate changes, but where is the evidence that net zero is going to stop it? Where is the evidence? There is no evidence.

“Climate change has always happened. It always will. Maybe the smarter thing to do is to adapt to it than think arrogantly that you can stop it.”

He added: “When it’s a bit warm, let’s enjoy it. And if it means that English wine and sparkling wine gets better and better, fantastic. That means we can take on the French – fantastic. Let’s celebrate some of these things rather than just be sort of doom and gloom about it.”

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Richard Tice’s comments are tone-deaf. With wildfires raging across the UK and drought threatening water supplies and food security, comments like these don’t just raise serious questions about his judgment – they also expose where his interests really lie.”

Tice’s comments came amid a record-breaking summer during which temperatures have risen above 35C several times, causing thousands of deaths, millions of hospital visits and costing the UK an estimated £4bn in economic output.

The government has estimated that 2,877 people died as a result of high temperatures during the May and June heatwaves – double the figure for the whole of last summer.

The climate breakdown has been linked to the increasing frequency of wildfires, which are burning larger areas across many parts of the world. The so-called firewave the UK witnessed weeks ago was the most widespread the country has seen, with the combination of wet winters and prolonged heatwaves exacerbating the risk.

A spokesperson for the Royal College of Nursing said: “Those calling for people to enjoy the impacts of climate change should say it to the nurses collapsing in hospitals where temperatures are hitting 36 degrees.

“Or to the thousands of patients lining corridors every day as extreme heat causes severe illness among the vulnerable, older people and even those without pre-existing conditions.

“Climate change is a public health emergency that’s getting worse in front of our eyes. The nursing profession doesn’t want out-of-touch interventions, but action to reduce emissions and make NHS and care facilities safe to work and be cared for in.”

Simon Williams, a public health researcher at Swansea University, said: “It’s concerning to see someone so high profile spreading misinformation around climate change and its impacts.

“Particularly for the elderly, heatwaves over time make them less capable of regulating their body temperature. Even a few degrees either way can have a major impact.”

The National Farmers’ Union, meanwhile, has said farmers are facing “one of the worst ever” harvests, while firefighters have battled wildfires in Derbyshire, the Midlands, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Reform has long campaigned to scrap the government’s commitment to reaching net zero by 2050 and has promised to end green subsidies if elected.

The party has taken tens of millions of pounds in donations from people with connections to the fossil fuel industry since it was set up in 2019, most notably from the billionaire Christopher Harborne, who owns a jet fuel brokerage and whose £5m gift to Nigel Farage is now at the centre of a parliamentary inquiry.

While Farage has questioned the role that human activity has played in changing the climate, his deputy leader has been more outspoken in denying that the planet is experiencing a climate crisis at all.

He posted in 2024: “We are not in climate emergency; nor is there a climate crisis. But yes, climate change is real because it has happened for millions of years past & will do in future.”

On Monday he called on the government to invest in desalination plants, which he said worked well in the Middle East, where he spends much of his time. “Where’s been the discussion about desalination plants that are used in other parts of the world very, very successfully?” he said.

“Yeah, there’s not much water on land in the Middle East. They use desalination plants. We’re surrounded by water. It is too difficult to build a reservoir – let’s look at desalination plants.”

Last week the Guardian reported that Thames Water was preparing to restart the UK’s only mainland desalination plant to restart operations later this year – but it will not be ready until the winter.

Alasdair Johnstone, the head of parliamentary engagement at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, said: “Far from being an enjoyable experience, for many this summer will have brought hardship, with 2,877 deaths during the May and June heatwaves, over 1,100 of which are directly attributable to the extra heat added by climate change.

“Firefighters have been called to over 1,000 wildfires, which have devastated the landscape, displaced people, and destroyed homes.

“The only way these climate change impacts can be prevented from becoming more common and severe is to tackle the cause, which means reaching net zero emissions by 2050.”

Amy Cameron, a programme director for Greenpeace UK, said: “Tice’s words show that a party bankrolled by fossil fuel interests will keep denying the climate crisis for its funders’ benefit even when its impacts are undeniable.

“Reform should try telling nurses fainting on shifts, farmers losing their crops and people running from burning homes to enjoy the hot weather and see what reaction they’ll get.”

People with severe intellectual disabilities live 24 years less on average

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 18:00:02 GMT

Exclusive: Research also finds stark ethnic disparities, and 40% of deaths among group classed as avoidable

People living with severe intellectual disabilities are dying 24 years younger on average than the wider population, a study has found, with 40% of such deaths being avoidable.

The study also found that within this group, people from minority ethnic backgrounds were dying 14 years younger than their white counterparts.

Researchers from King’s College London analysed data from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) and the LeDeR programme of 1,301 adults with severe or profound intellectual disability who died in England between 2021 and 2023.

They then compared this with 2,626 adults with a mild or moderate intellectual disability and 536,311 adults from the general population who died in 2022.

People with severe or profound intellectual disability died at an average age of 58, compared with 65 for those with a mild or moderate intellectual disability and 82 for the general population.

Two in five of the first group’s deaths were judged to be avoidable. Avoidable deaths were defined as deaths occurring before the age of 75 due to preventable or treatable causes.

Pneumonia and epilepsy were the leading avoidable causes, notably higher than in the other two groups, followed by cerebrovascular disease (concerning blood flow and blood vessels in the brain).

Jon Sparkes, the chief executive of learning disability charity Mencap, called the findings shocking but “sadly unsurprising”. “Much more must be done to ensure people with the most complex needs can access care,” he said.

“Organisational failings were identified in more than 40% of deaths reviewed last year, showing the way the NHS just isn’t designed to work for people with a learning disability.

“This research shows why it is so vital that that the government and NHS consider and meet the needs of people with a learning disability, whether in the new neighbourhood health schemes, through work on moving the NHS to be more digital, or preventing poor health. Only by doing this will we address and end the deep-rooted healthcare inequalities that are cutting lives short.”

The analysis also found stark ethnic disparities. Within the group of people living with severe or profound intellectual disabilities, those from Black, Asian and other minority ethnic backgrounds were likely to die significantly sooner than their white peers, with a 14-year disparity.

According to the researchers, this variance may highlight additional challenges in accessing healthcare encountered by people from ethnic minorities, and also reflects how compounding inequalities exacerbate the already poorer health outcomes people with disabilities face.

Dr Michael Kwan Leung Yu, the first author of the study and a postdoctoral research associate at King’s College, said: “LeDeR provides a unique national lens that no single trust or region can offer. Its scale allows us, for the first time, to examine avoidable deaths among adults with severe or profound intellectual disabilities through a population-based analysis and explore this in greater detail.

“The findings point to a need for targeted interventions, including annual health checks, vaccination programmes and timely management of conditions such as pneumonia and epilepsy, reaching adults with severe or profound intellectual disability consistently, with particular attention to those from ethnic minority backgrounds.”

Dr Rory Sheehan, a co-first author of the study and senior clinical lecturer at King’s institute of psychiatry, psychology and neuroscience, said: “Pneumonia and epilepsy are largely treatable, so seeing them as leading causes of avoidable death in this group points to a gap between the care people could receive and the care they are getting.

“Closing that gap means making sure basic interventions, health checks, vaccination [and] timely treatment reliably reach adults with severe or profound intellectual disability.”

It’s time for freakishly gifted Harry Brook to come of age in England’s post-Bazball era

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 18:00:01 GMT

Test captaincy came too soon for 27-year-old but Pakistan series is latest chapter in year that could be the making of him

You have to hand it to Bazball. Even when seemingly killed off, and the England team it left behind is thousands of miles away, preparing for a series against Pakistan, it has still managed to muscle its way into the fallout from Bangladesh’s seismic victory over Australia in Darwin. Talk about main character energy.

By definition, that nine-wicket victory for Bangladesh was no fluke. Najmul Hossain Shanto’s men didn’t jag a tight one but rather dominated their hosts over four days. And in doing so, they also managed to unite Ashes rivals by demonstrating what a golden opportunity England blew against Australia’s greybeards last winter.

To say as much back then was to risk being called as deluded as the team itself; to be an enabler of the hubris that underpinned England’s gung-ho approach. Stuart Broad, for example, was widely lampooned for saying that Australia, though an excellent side, were ageing and as vulnerable as they had been for a long time.

But plenty of Australian voices are now making the same point, either directly or by implication. A common refrain has been that, had England batted “sensibly” – ie with the same gimlet-eyed application of Bangladesh in a match-defining 400-plus total amassed over 138 overs – that sorry 4-1 defeat could have been very different.

While England’s bowling has been forgotten here – Bangladesh opted against feeding Travis Head’s cut shot like it was a goose being fattened for foie gras – thoughts certainly do go back to the defining collapses in Perth and Brisbane, when a string of batters hardwired to attack ignored the risk that seemed so obvious.

Among them was Harry Brook, whose most recent act in the whites of England was to go down swinging against New Zealand and trigger another wave of chuntering about there being more brains in a pork pie. Brook was following team orders but all people saw was 21 off nine balls and yet another example of Harry-kiri.

In a parallel universe Brook is about to captain England’s Test team for the first time at his home ground of Headingley this week. Instead, England have turned back to Joe Root as the successor to Ben Stokes, with Rob Key saying the vacancy had come “too soon” for Brook and hinting that greater maturity was needed.

Perhaps it was too great an ask for Brook to lead across all three formats, or too messy to hive off the T20 captaincy to another player under split coaches. Of course the unsaid bit here is that nightclub incident in Wellington last November – the spark for the chain reaction that ultimately created the vacancy.

Although beyond learning that knocking back hazy pale ales the night before captaining in a one-day international is probably a bad idea, how much does Brook actually need to change his approach?

Clearly driving on the up in unfamiliar Perth was not smart from Brook, likewise trying to larrup Mitchell Starc under lights in his first pink-ball Test. Overall his Ashes was disappointing and a year has passed since his last Test century – a period in which wicketkeepers Alex Carey and Tom Blundell standing up to the quicks has caused him issues.

But as much as the removal of Brendon McCullum as England’s Test head coach after the 2-1 defeat by New Zealand signals a desire for the pendulum to swing back a touch overall, Brook feels the very least of their problems right now. The fact is, for all that his dismissals can be triggering in the moment, Brook has already put up the kind of numbers that mark him out as a truly remarkable talent. After 38 Tests he averages 53, has scored 10 centuries (including a triple in Multan), and he sits second in the Test batting rankings behind Head.

As per the good people at CricViz, Brook has achieved this by trying to smack 44% of deliveries to or over the boundary – a figure only Head can match. More broadly, the 27-year-old looks to score off 65% of balls he faces, and defend or leave 35%. The average split for top-seven batters since his debut in 2022 has been 52/48.

after newsletter promotion

The lazy assumption is that this has been achieved on flat pitches. But while true Brook is lethal in these conditions – Pakistan know better than anyone, victims of four Brook centuries on home soil, including that career-best 317 – like Head, he can come into his own when the ball is doing plenty for the bowlers.

His century in Wellington in late 2024 is a prime example, compiled from just 91 balls, and on an opening day when 15 wickets tumbled. A personal view is that he should have been player of the match in Melbourne last winter, with his 41 on the opening day of that crapshoot absolutely central to the end result.

Charlie Dean will captain England in next month’s three one-day internationals against Ireland in the absence of Nat Sciver-Brunt.

Dean stood in for Sciver-Brunt during white-ball series against New Zealand and India this summer then again when the all-rounder was injured during the group stage of the T20 World Cup.

Sciver-Brunt is continuing to manage her fitness and recovery, as is Danni Wyatt-Hodge, so they will miss the Ireland series, alongside fellow senior players Sophie Ecclestone, Lauren Bell and Amy Jones.

England squad to face Ireland: C Dean (captain), M Bouchier, A Capsey, K Chathli, T Corteen-Coleman, S Dunkley, L Filer, D Gibson, J Grewcock, F Kemp, R MacDonald-Gay, C Pavely, G Potts, M Villiers, I Wong.

Naturally people still want more. Stokes even took Brook aside at the end of that Ashes series and told him he should be averaging “65, even 70” in Test cricket. The diagnosis here was that Brook, like a lot of modern players, has a 360-degree armoury of shots but is still learning when and where to deploy them.

For AB de Villiers, whose remarkable hand-eye ability was comparable to Brook, it similarly comes down to risk assessment; being able to spot when the odds are against him and, whether it is five deliveries or an hour, holding firm until it flips in his favour. “Definitely don’t lose the aggressive nature of your batting or the creative side,” De Villiers told For The Love of Cricket. “Just earn the right.”

As per a recent chat with BBC Sport, Brook acknowledges this and gets as frustrated as the next person at some of his dismissals. But his stated aim is still to be a matchwinner for England first and foremost. “I have the ability to hit it everywhere, I just have to figure it out quicker in games,” he said.

Some supporters may recoil at this but really they should be encouraged. As much as the excesses of Bazball squandered a golden chance in Australia, overall it allowed the freakishly gifted Brook to discover the limits of what is possible. Avoid an over-correction and this tricky last year could yet be the making of him.

Ministers drop plan to relax affordable housing rules after negative response

The Guardian Mon, 17 Aug 2026 17:45:17 GMT

Government concedes ‘significant opposition’ requires new approach on quotas for medium-sized development sites

Ministers have dropped plans to relax affordable housing rules for developers in England after a backlash from housing experts who warned it could drastically cut the number of cheaper homes available in rural areas.

The government said on Monday it would not go ahead with proposals to end affordable housing quotas for private builders on sites containing between 10 and 49 houses after a consultation triggered an overwhelmingly negative response.

The change, which was included in the government’s 150-page planning reform document (pdf) on Monday, is one of the most significant reversals ministers have made to housing policy since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

Kate Henderson, the chief executive of the National Housing Federation (NHF), said: “It’s extremely positive to see that the government has listened to the social housing sector and decided against removing onsite affordable housing requirements on medium-sized development sites.

“This decision will safeguard one of the most important routes for delivering social homes in rural areas, ensuring we can build genuinely affordable homes where people need them, in every postcode across the country.”

Under the original proposals, ministers would have allowed developers to make cash payments instead of building affordable housing on-site if their developments were between 10 and 49 houses.

Ministers hoped the measures might help to boost sluggish rates of housebuilding and bring the government closer to its target of building 1.5m new homes by the end of this parliament. The Treasury under Rachel Reeves is understood to have been particularly keen on the idea.

Housing experts, however, warned that such a rule change would have a major impact, especially in rural areas where a significant number of affordable homes are built on medium sites rather than larger ones.

An analysis of government statistics by the NHF, revealed by the Guardian, showed that in the most rural areas of England, more than half of all affordable homes are built on developments of this size.

The organisation said the policy change could cost the country 32,000 affordable homes over the next 10 years.

The government document reveals that of the 910 people and groups who responded to the consultation, 41% were strongly opposed to the measure, compared with just 18% who were strongly in favour.

The document said: “There was significant opposition across stakeholder groups.”

It added: “The government has considered these responses and has decided not to proceed with proposals to allow applicants discretion to deliver social and affordable housing requirements via cash payments in lieu of on-site delivery on medium sites.

“This reflects concerns that, at this time, it could have a detrimental impact on the manifesto commitment to deliver the biggest increase in social and affordable housebuilding in a generation and to strengthen planning obligations to ensure new developments provide more affordable homes.”

Ministers are keen to relax regulations for private sector builders in other ways. Moves announced on Monday included instructing councils to give a “default yes” approach to housing developments that are within a reasonable walking distance of well-connected train and tram stations.

Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, said on Monday: “I’m very clear that we need these homes. We have already seen nearly 400,000 since we came into office, new homes that have completed. We’ve seen a 15% increase in start-ups for housing starts.

“We want to continue on that path and that’s why we’ve set out these rules to make sure that we can get planning through as quickly as possible, and we can get the infrastructure alongside the housing that we desperately need.”
